stem: Which statement best describes user-centred design?
options: The client's budget and deadline decide each design choice, and users see the final product
The developer designs the interface, and users take part only once beta testing begins
Users' needs and feedback guide design decisions throughout the development of the solution
Screens follow the programming language's standard templates so that every solution looks alike
explanation: User-centred design puts the people who will use the solution at the centre: their needs shape the design, and their feedback is sought and acted on throughout development.
whyWrong: Budget and deadline are constraints; a design that ignores users until the end isn't user-centred.
Involving users only at beta testing is too late for their needs to shape the design.
Standard templates suit the developer's convenience, not the needs of a particular group of users.

stem: Quenda Plumbing in Shepparton updates its job-logging app. The update adds a drop-down list of common job types and fills in the date and the technician's name automatically. Technicians now log a job in 40 seconds instead of two minutes, and the job records are as accurate as before. Which statement best describes the update?
options: It improves efficiency, because each job takes less time and effort to log
It improves effectiveness, because each job takes less time and effort to log
It improves effectiveness, because the job records are now more accurate
It improves efficiency, because the job records now contain more detail
explanation: Logging a job now takes less time and fewer keystrokes, which is a gain in efficiency. The records are no more accurate than before, so the update can't be credited with an accuracy gain.
whyWrong: Time and effort are measures of efficiency, not effectiveness.
The scenario says the records are as accurate as before, so accuracy hasn't improved.
Nothing suggests more detail is recorded, and completeness would be a measure of effectiveness.

stem: Kalinda is developing a medication-reminder app for residents of Marlock House, an aged-care home in Warragul. Which action best reflects user-centred design?
options: Asking the home's IT manager to approve the colour scheme before coding begins
Watching residents use an early version and changing screens where they struggle
Choosing the code library that lets her finish the app in the shortest time
Writing pseudocode for every module before speaking with any of the residents
explanation: Observing the actual users with an early version, and revising the design where they have difficulty, puts the residents' needs at the centre of development.
whyWrong: The IT manager isn't a user of the app; a manager's approval doesn't show that the design suits residents.
Choosing tools for the developer's speed may make development quicker, but it doesn't involve users.
Designing every module without consulting residents is the opposite of user-centred design.

stem: A developer at Pipi Beach Couriers in Warrnambool changes the invoicing module so that it rechecks every total against the rate table before saving. Invoicing a day's jobs now takes 12 minutes instead of 5, and the pricing errors that used to appear on about 1 in 50 invoices have stopped. Which evaluation of the change is most accurate?
options: Efficiency has improved, because every total is now checked before saving
Efficiency and effectiveness have both improved, because errors have stopped
Effectiveness is unchanged, because an invoice is still produced for every job
Effectiveness has improved, but efficiency has fallen, as invoicing takes longer
explanation: The module's purpose is to produce correct invoices. Stopping the pricing errors means it achieves that purpose more accurately, so effectiveness has improved. Invoicing now takes 12 minutes instead of 5, which uses more time, so efficiency has fallen.
whyWrong: Checking totals improves accuracy, a measure of effectiveness, and the extra time means efficiency has fallen.
Invoicing takes 12 minutes instead of 5, so efficiency has fallen, not improved.
Producing an invoice isn't enough; the invoices are now more accurate, so effectiveness has improved.

stem: Priya updates the order-entry module used by phone staff at Goldfinch Lane Produce, a fruit and vegetable wholesaler in Shepparton. Staff used to type each product name in full; now the module suggests matching products once the first three letters are typed. The owner wants to know whether the change has made the module more *effective*, by comparing a measurement taken before and after the change. Which measurement should be compared?
options: The average time staff take to enter an order
The number of orders per 100 that list a wrong product
The average number of keystrokes needed to enter an order
The staff wages spent on taking phone orders each week
explanation: Effectiveness is how well the module achieves its purpose: recording what the customer actually ordered. The number of orders that list a wrong product measures accuracy, so it shows whether effectiveness has changed. Time, keystrokes and wage costs are measures of efficiency.
whyWrong: Time taken to complete a task is a measure of efficiency, not effectiveness.
Keystrokes measure the effort a task needs, which is a measure of efficiency.
Wages spent reflect time and cost, which are measures of efficiency.

stem: Ruby developed a spray-record app for Mulga Bend Table Grapes in Mildura, working on her office computer. After the app was released, she learnt that workers record each spray out in the vineyard, on a phone, in bright sunlight and often out of mobile range. Many of them can't read the screen, and sprays recorded out of range are never saved. Under user-centred design, which activity would most likely have revealed these problems earliest?
options: Alpha testing each module against a test table before release
Beta testing a near-final version with a group of the workers
Surveying the workers about the app a month after it was released
Watching workers record sprays in the vineyard before designing
explanation: User-centred design begins by finding out who the users are, what tasks they do and where they do them. Watching workers in the vineyard before designing would have shown the bright sunlight and the patchy mobile coverage, so the screens, and the way records are saved, could have been designed for those conditions from the start.
whyWrong: Alpha testing is done by the developers, usually away from the vineyard, so it checks the app's processing rather than the conditions it is used in.
Beta testing with the workers would probably reveal the problems, but only once the app is nearly finished, when redesigning it takes much more work.
A survey after release finds the problems only once the app is in use, which is when Ruby found them.

stem: Gang-gang Electrical in Healesville uses a quoting program. Staff build each quote by choosing items from a list of about 400 items and entering the labour hours. Which change would improve the program's efficiency without reducing its effectiveness?
options: Showing the items quoted most often at the top of the item list
Removing the check that each quote's total matches its listed items
Asking staff to retype each quote's total on a second screen to confirm it
Leaving labour off each quote so that quotes are faster to prepare
explanation: Putting the most common items first cuts the time and effort needed to build a quote, which improves efficiency. Each quote still lists the same items and is just as accurate and complete, so effectiveness isn't reduced.
whyWrong: Quotes would be quicker to finish, but a total that doesn't match its items could reach a customer, so effectiveness falls.
Retyping every total adds time and effort to each quote, which reduces efficiency.
A quote without labour is incomplete and understates the price, so effectiveness falls.

stem: Emu Bush Community Garden in Horsham has a plot-booking program that holds bookings in an array of records while it runs. Members report that bookings made yesterday disappeared after the program was closed and reopened. What is the most likely cause?
options: The bookings were saved in a CSV file instead of an XML file
The bookings were held only in the array and never written to a file
The booking dates were stored as Strings instead of as Integers
The array held records instead of a two-dimensional array of values
explanation: An array exists in memory only while the program runs. Unless the bookings are written to a file before the program closes, they are lost.
whyWrong: A CSV file keeps its data between runs, just as an XML file does.
The data type of a field doesn't decide whether the data survives the program closing.
Any structure held in memory is lost when the program closes, so the choice of structure isn't the cause.

stem: Pickaxe Lane Hardware in Maldon keeps its stock list in `stock.csv`. The table shows the fields in each line, with an example value. When the program reads a line, it stores the fields in a record. Which data types best suit `onHand`, `price` and `discontinued`, in that order?
options: Integer, Integer, Character
Floating point, Floating point, String
Integer, Floating point, Boolean
String, Floating point, Boolean
explanation: `onHand` counts whole items, so Integer suits. `price` includes cents, so Floating point suits. `discontinued` has only two possible states, so Boolean suits.
whyWrong: An Integer can't hold cents, and a two-state value suits Boolean rather than Character.
A stock count is a whole number, and a String can't be tested directly as true or false.
A stock count stored as a String can't be added to or subtracted from without conversion.

figures.title: Fields in each line of stock.csv

stem: Ovens Bend Outdoor Supplies in Bright stores its stock in a CSV file. A program reads one line of the file and splits it into the array `fields`; the algorithm shown sets `fields` to the result. Every value read from the file is a String. Arrays are indexed from 0. What does the algorithm display?
explanation: `onShelf` holds the String "12" and `inStoreroom` holds the String "5". With Strings, `+` joins the values, so the algorithm displays 125. Converting both to Integer first would display 17.
whyWrong: 17 would be displayed only if both values were converted to Integer before being added.
Joining Strings with `+` doesn't insert a space between them.
This joins `fields[0]` and `fields[1]`, treating the array as if it were indexed from 1.

figures.code:
BEGIN
    fields ← ["BK-204", "12", "5"]
    onShelf ← fields[1]
    inStoreroom ← fields[2]
    DISPLAY onShelf + inStoreroom
END

stem: Sugar Glider Athletics Club in Ararat must send each carnival's results to the state association's system. Each event has a different number of competitors, and the association plans to add new fields to the results next season. Which output format best suits?
options: An XML file, because nested elements with named tags can vary in number and be extended
A CSV file, because every record has the same fields, which are separated by commas
A plain text file, because any program can open it and display its contents to a user
A two-dimensional array, because it stores events in rows and competitors in columns
explanation: XML lets each event element contain any number of competitor elements, and its self-describing tags let new fields be added without breaking programs that read the existing ones.
whyWrong: CSV is flat and identifies fields only by their position, so it can't nest competitors within events, and adding new fields could break the association's program.
Plain text has no field structure, so the association's system couldn't reliably extract the results.
An array exists only in a program's memory; it isn't a file format that can be sent to another system.

stem: Blue Loam Potatoes, a grower near Thorpdale, keeps its yields in `yields.csv`, shown below. Each line holds one paddock's yields, in tonnes, for four seasons, and there is no header row. The program reads line 1 into row 0 of the two-dimensional array `yields[paddock][season]`, line 2 into row 1, and so on, converting each field to Integer. Arrays are indexed from 0. Which element holds the value 29?
options: `yields[2][1]`
`yields[2][3]`
`yields[1][2]`
`yields[3][2]`
explanation: 29 is on line 2 of the file, which is stored in row 1, and it is the third field on that line, which is at index 2. The row index comes first, so the element is `yields[1][2]`.
whyWrong: This puts the field before the line: `yields[2][1]` is row 2 (line 3), index 1, which holds 53.
This counts from 1: with indexes from 0, `yields[2][3]` is the fourth field of line 3, which holds 46.
This counts from 1 and puts the field first; the rows are indexed 0 to 2, so there is no row 3.

stem: The data dictionary shown is part of the design for a harvest report at Spinifex Bend Almonds in Robinvale. The program reads each block's details from a file, calculates the average harvest per tree, and outputs a report. Which change should be made to the data dictionary?
options: Change `avgKg` to Floating point
Change `totalKg` to Integer
Change `treeCount` to Floating point
Change `irrigated` to String
explanation: `avgKg` is calculated by division, so it usually has a fractional part: 18462.5 ÷ 640 is about 28.8. An Integer can't hold that value or report it to one decimal place, so `avgKg` should be Floating point.
whyWrong: Harvest weights such as 18462.5 kg include part kilograms, so Floating point suits `totalKg`.
Trees are counted in whole numbers, so Integer suits `treeCount`.
Whether a block is irrigated has only two states, so Boolean suits `irrigated`.

figures.title: Data dictionary (extract)
rows: Name of the block, e.g. North 3
Number of trees in the block, e.g. 640
Kilograms harvested from the block, e.g. 18462.5
Average kilograms per tree (totalKg ÷ treeCount), reported to one decimal place

stem: Ringtail Couriers in Ballarat charges a delivery fee that depends on the suburb. Its delivery program holds each suburb and its fee in an array of records that is written into the program's code. The fees change every few months, and each change needs a developer to edit the code and release a new version. The office manager wants to update the fees herself. Which change best meets this need?
options: Declare each suburb's fee as a named constant at the top of the code
Hold the suburbs and fees in a two-dimensional array instead of records
Have staff type the delivery fee into a text box for every order
Read the suburbs and fees from a file that the manager can edit
explanation: Data that changes often is better kept in a data source outside the code. If the program reads the suburbs and fees from a file, such as a CSV file, each time it starts, the manager can change a fee in the file and the program uses the new fee on its next run, with no change to the code. The program should still validate what it reads, because an edited file can contain mistakes.
whyWrong: A constant is still part of the code, so each fee change would still need a developer to edit the program and release it again.
This changes only how the data is organised; a two-dimensional array written into the code still has to be edited by a developer.
Typing a fee for every order adds time and effort, and fees typed from memory can be wrong or inconsistent.

stem: A booking form must let a customer choose exactly one of three fixed delivery methods. Which GUI control is most suitable?
options: A group of check boxes
A single-line text box
A single command button
A group of radio buttons
explanation: Radio buttons show every option and allow only one to be selected, which matches choosing exactly one of a few fixed methods.
whyWrong: Check boxes allow several options to be selected at once.
A text box lets the customer type anything, so misspelt or invalid methods could be entered.
A button triggers an action when clicked; it doesn't record a choice.

stem: Tallowwood Hollow Nursery in Bairnsdale uses the function shown to calculate the cost of sending an online order. What does `shippingCost(8, TRUE)` return?
explanation: 8 is greater than 5, so line 5 sets `cost` to 9.50 + 3 × 1.20 = 13.10. `express` is TRUE, so line 8 doubles it to 26.20, which is returned.
whyWrong: 13.10 is the cost before line 8 doubles it for express delivery.
19.00 doubles the rate on line 3, but line 3 runs only when the weight is 5 or less.
38.20 multiplies the whole weight by 1.20 instead of only the 3 above 5.

figures.code:
FUNCTION shippingCost(weight, express)
    IF weight ≤ 5 THEN
        cost ← 9.50
    ELSE
        cost ← 9.50 + (weight - 5) * 1.20
    ENDIF
    IF express = TRUE THEN
        cost ← cost * 2
    ENDIF
    RETURN cost
ENDFUNCTION

stem: Juniper is developing an ordering program for Mudlark Deliveries in Echuca. She copied the same 12 lines that calculate a delivery fee into four event handlers. When the fee rule changed to include a $10 minimum, she updated three of the copies but missed the fourth, so some customers were undercharged. Which approach would best have prevented this error?
options: Writing the calculation once as a function that each event handler calls
Storing the per-kilometre rate in a global variable that every handler reads
Adding a comment beside each copy of the calculation to explain its purpose
Setting a breakpoint in each handler to check the fee while the program runs
explanation: With the calculation in one function, the new $10 minimum would be written once and every handler would use it. Each copy of duplicated code must be changed separately, and one can be missed.
whyWrong: A shared rate helps only when the rate changes; here the rule changed, and the calculation was still copied four times.
Comments explain code but don't stop copies of it from getting out of step.
Breakpoints help find an error during testing; they don't prevent the duplicated code that caused it.

stem: Wattle Wagon Toy Library in Hamilton calculates late fees with the function `lateFee` and the algorithm shown. Arrays are indexed from 0. What does the algorithm display?
explanation: `lateFee(0)` returns 0, because neither condition is true. `lateFee(3)` returns 5. `lateFee(10)` returns 5 + 3 × 2 = 11. The total is 0 + 5 + 11 = 16.
whyWrong: 11 is only the fee for 10 days; the loop adds all three fees to `total`.
21 charges $5 for 0 days, but `days > 0` is FALSE when `days` is 0.
10 charges the flat $5 for 10 days, but `days > 7` is checked first and is TRUE.

figures.title: Function lateFee
figures.code:
FUNCTION lateFee(days)
    fee ← 0
    IF days > 7 THEN
        fee ← 5 + (days - 7) * 2
    ELSEIF days > 0 THEN
        fee ← 5
    ENDIF
    RETURN fee
ENDFUNCTION

figures.title: Algorithm
figures.code:
BEGIN
    daysLate ← [0, 3, 10]
    total ← 0
    FOR i ← 0 TO 2
        total ← total + lateFee(daysLate[i])
    ENDFOR
    DISPLAY total
END

stem: Oystercatcher Point Kayak Hire in Metung calculates hire costs with the function shown, in which every seventh day of a hire is free. Callum wants the cost of an 8-day hire at $45 a day, so he writes `total ← hireCost(45, 8)`. What value does `total` receive?
explanation: Arguments are passed to parameters in order, so `days` receives 45 and `dailyRate` receives 8. Line 2 sets `freeDays` to 45 DIV 7 = 6, and line 3 sets `cost` to (45 − 6) × 8 = 312. Callum should have written `hireCost(8, 45)`, which returns (8 − 1) × 45 = 315.
whyWrong: 315 is what Callum intended, but arguments are matched to parameters by position, not by meaning, so `days` receives 45.
352 takes one free day, as for an 8-day hire, but `days` is 45, so 45 DIV 7 gives 6 free days.
360 leaves out the free days, but line 2 sets `freeDays` to 6 and line 3 subtracts them.

figures.code:
FUNCTION hireCost(days, dailyRate)
    freeDays ← days DIV 7
    cost ← (days - freeDays) * dailyRate
    RETURN cost
ENDFUNCTION

stem: The weather station at Pelican Point Sailing Club on Lake Boga records the wind speed every half hour. At the end of each day, the array `wind` holds that day's 48 readings, oldest first. Arrays are indexed from 0. An end-of-day summary must show the day's last six readings, newest first. The body of each loop below is `DISPLAY wind[i]`. Which loop is correct?
options: `FOR i ← 42 TO 47`
`FOR i ← 48 TO 43 STEP -1`
`FOR i ← 47 TO 41 STEP -1`
`FOR i ← 47 TO 42 STEP -1`
explanation: With 48 readings indexed from 0, the newest is at index 47, and the last six are at indexes 42 to 47. Counting down from 47 to 42 with `STEP -1` displays them newest first, and because both bounds are inclusive, the loop runs exactly six times.
whyWrong: This displays the right six readings, but oldest first, because index 42 holds the earliest of them.
This counts as if the array were indexed from 1. Index 48 doesn't exist, so the first pass causes an index out of range error.
Counting down from 47 to 41 displays seven readings, one more than the six required.

stem: On the online order form for Woodfire Wren Pizza in Myrtleford, the price shown must update as soon as the customer picks a different pizza size from a drop-down list. Which is the most suitable way to program this?
options: Run a loop that checks the drop-down list over and over for a new size
Link a procedure that recalculates the price to the list's change event
Store the chosen size in a global variable that every procedure can read
Recalculate the price only when the customer clicks the Order button
explanation: GUI programs are event-driven. Choosing a new size raises the drop-down list's change event, and the procedure linked to that event (its event handler) recalculates and displays the price straight away.
whyWrong: Checking the list over and over wastes processing; a GUI program runs code when an event happens instead.
A global variable can hold the size, but storing it doesn't make any code run when the size changes.
The price would update only when the order is placed, not when the size changes, as required.

stem: What is the main purpose of a code repository in a software development project?
options: To supply pre-written functions that the program calls to do common tasks
To let the program request data from a service run by another organisation
To store the project's code and its history of changes for the team to share
To generate new code automatically from a description of what is needed
explanation: A repository stores source code with a history of every change, so team members can share code, see who changed what and return to earlier versions.
whyWrong: This describes a code library.
This describes an API.
This describes an AI-based coding assistant.

stem: Currawong Community Bus in Bendigo has an app that shows where each bus is on a map, using a third-party mapping API. The provider announces that free access will end in 60 days, after which every request will need a paid key. Which response best manages this risk?
options: Save the provider's map images in the app's repository so that they can be reused later
Compare the new fee with other providers, then update the module that calls the API
Remove the map and have drivers type their locations into a CSV file every hour
Leave the code unchanged, because the map feature has already passed alpha testing
explanation: The change is a known risk of depending on an API. Weighing the fee against other providers, then changing only the module that calls the API, keeps the feature working before free access ends.
whyWrong: Copying the provider's images is likely to breach its terms of use, and the saved maps would soon be out of date.
Typing locations once an hour would make them late and less accurate, reducing the app's effectiveness.
Passing earlier tests doesn't protect the app; once free access ends, its requests will fail.

stem: Dan finds an open-source charting library he could use in a reporting program for Hopkins Flats Dairy Co-op in Warrnambool. Which check is most important before he includes it in the program?
options: That its licence allows this use, and what acknowledgement it requires
That its functions follow the same naming convention as Dan's own code
That its source code has been rewritten as pseudocode for the design
That it reads its data from XML files rather than from CSV files
explanation: A library's licence sets the conditions for using it, such as whether it may be included in the co-op's program and how its authors must be acknowledged. Ignoring the licence can infringe the authors' rights.
whyWrong: Naming conventions affect readability; they aren't a condition of using the library.
Pseudocode is a design tool for the developer's own modules; a library doesn't need to be rewritten.
The file format a library reads doesn't decide whether it may be used.

stem: An app for Thornbill Rise Orchard in Harcourt shows a frost forecast using data from a weather API. The temperature used to arrive in a `<temp>` element. Without warning, the provider renamed it `<temperature>`, and the app now shows a blank forecast. The app's code hasn't changed. Which statement best explains the failure?
options: A syntax error was introduced the last time the app's code was translated
The weather library's licence expired, so its functions were switched off
The code repository rolled the app back to an earlier version of its code
The app depends on a data format that the provider controls and changed
explanation: The app looks for an element named `temp`. The provider controls the API's data format; when it renamed the element, the app could no longer find the value, even though the app's own code was unchanged.
whyWrong: The code hasn't changed, and a syntax error would stop the code being translated rather than blank one value.
The app uses an online API, not a library, and nothing suggests a licence has expired.
A repository doesn't change code by itself, and the app's code is unchanged.

stem: The developers at Tambo Crossing Software in Bairnsdale keep the code for a council's parking permit system in a shared code repository. Which commit message would be most useful to a team member reading the history months later?
options: Friday afternoon's work on the permit reminders module
Fixed the bug that Sam found in testing
Updated the reminders module and several other files
Reminders now sent 30 days before expiry, not 14
explanation: The repository already records who made each commit, when, and which files changed. The message should say what the change does, so anyone reading the history can find the commit that changed a rule, check it, and roll it back if needed.
whyWrong: The repository already records when each commit was made, and this message doesn't say what changed.
It doesn't say which bug was fixed or how, so the history can't be searched for the change.
The repository already records which files changed; the message should say what the change does.

stem: The invoicing program at Bindi Creek Plumbing Supplies in Sale uses a charting library. A developer upgraded the library to its newest version and released the program to staff the same day. The new version had renamed a function that the program calls, so the monthly sales chart stopped working. Which practice would have stopped the failure reaching staff?
options: Replacing the library with an online API that its provider keeps up to date
Testing the program with the new version before releasing it to staff
Committing the invoicing code to the repository more often
Range checking the sales figures before passing them to the chart
explanation: With a library, the developer decides when to upgrade. Re-testing the program with the new version before releasing it, and keeping the working version until then, would have found the renamed function during testing, before staff were affected.
whyWrong: An online API can be changed by its provider at any time, so the same failure could happen without the developer upgrading anything.
Frequent commits make it easier to roll back, but the failure would still reach staff before anyone noticed it.
Validation checks the data; it can't detect that a library function has been renamed.

stem: The booking page for Ghost Crab Cruises in Cowes shows a marine weather forecast from a third-party API. The free plan allows 1000 requests a day, and the page requests the forecast every time a customer opens it. On busy days, requests start failing by early afternoon and the forecast goes blank. The provider updates its forecast every three hours. Which change best solves the problem?
options: Request the forecast every 30 minutes, store it and show the stored copy
Move every call to the API into a single module that the page calls
Show a message asking customers to check the forecast again tomorrow
Request the forecast twice each time the page is opened, in case one fails
explanation: The page uses up the daily limit because it sends a request on every visit. Requesting the forecast every 30 minutes uses 48 requests a day, and showing the stored copy gives every customer a forecast. Because the provider updates its forecast only every three hours, the stored copy is never far behind, provided the plan's terms allow the forecast to be stored.
whyWrong: Keeping the API calls in one module makes a change to the API easier to handle, but the page would still send a request on every visit.
Customers would still see no forecast, so the feature would fail its purpose on busy days.
Doubling the requests uses up the daily limit twice as fast.

stem: An online order form for Seedpod Nursery in Kyneton asks customers to type their state or territory into a text box. Many entries are misspelt. Which change would most reduce the validation this field needs?
options: Storing the state in a Character variable instead of a String variable
Replacing the text box with a drop-down list of the states and territories
Adding a debugging output statement that displays the state after entry
Making the text box wider so that longer state names are fully visible
explanation: A drop-down list offers only valid states and territories, so misspelt or invalid entries can't be made. Only an existence check, confirming that a state has been chosen, is still needed.
whyWrong: A Character holds a single character, so it can't store a state name, and it wouldn't stop misspellings.
Debugging output helps a developer find errors; it doesn't stop users entering invalid data.
A wider box changes the layout, not what the user can type.

stem: Redgum Flat Junior Cricket Club in Donald accepts players aged 5 to 17 inclusive. Which condition is TRUE exactly when an entered age is invalid?
options: `age < 5 AND age > 17`
`age ≤ 5 OR age ≥ 17`
`age > 5 OR age < 17`
`age < 5 OR age > 17`
explanation: An age is invalid if it is below 5 or above 17. `OR` makes the condition TRUE when either is the case, and the strict `<` and `>` keep the boundary ages 5 and 17 valid.
whyWrong: No age is both below 5 and above 17, so this is never TRUE and every age is accepted.
`≤` and `≥` make the valid boundary ages 5 and 17 count as invalid.
Every age is either above 5 or below 17, so this is always TRUE and every age is rejected.

stem: Tarwin Tide Egg Farm in Tarwin Lower sells eggs online in orders of 1 to 12 trays. The algorithm shown checks the number of trays. A customer enters 13, then 0, then 12, then 5. How many times is the message on line 4 displayed, and what does line 7 display?
options: Twice; then `Order: 12 trays`
Three times; then `Order: 5 trays`
Once; then `Order: 12 trays`
Twice; then `Order: 5 trays`
explanation: 13 fails the check, so the message is displayed and 0 is read. 0 also fails, so the message is displayed again and 12 is read. 12 passes, so the loop ends and line 7 displays `Order: 12 trays`; 5 is never read.
whyWrong: 12 is valid, so the loop ends after it is read; 5 is never read and 12 is never rejected.
0 is below 1, so it fails the check and the message is displayed a second time.
The message count is right, but the loop ends when 12 is entered, so 5 is never read.

figures.code:
BEGIN
    INPUT trays
    WHILE trays < 1 OR trays > 12 DO
        DISPLAY "Enter 1 to 12 trays"
        INPUT trays
    ENDWHILE
    DISPLAY "Order: " + trays + " trays"
END

stem: Kooyoora Rainfall Group in Wedderburn imports members' daily readings from a CSV file. One line holds `ERR` in the rainfall field instead of a number, and the import program crashes when it converts that field. Which technique would best prevent this?
options: Setting a breakpoint on the line of code that reads each record from the file
Storing every rainfall reading as a String so that any value can be read in
Type checking each rainfall field as it is read, and reporting invalid lines
Range checking each rainfall reading after the monthly totals are calculated
explanation: A type check applied as each line is read finds the non-numeric field before it is converted, so the program can skip and report that line instead of crashing.
whyWrong: A breakpoint helps a developer inspect the program during testing; it doesn't stop the crash when the program is used.
Readings stored as Strings can't be totalled, so the problem simply moves to the calculation.
The crash happens when the field is converted, before any totals exist, and a range check doesn't detect text.

stem: Bilby Burrow Party Rooms in Wangaratta takes party bookings for 10 to 30 children. Parties are held in the small room or the large room, and the small room holds at most 15 children. The room is chosen with radio buttons, so `room` is always "small" or "large". Which condition is TRUE exactly when a booking is valid?
options: `(children ≥ 10 AND children ≤ 30) OR (room = "small" AND children ≤ 15)`
`(children ≥ 10 OR children ≤ 30) AND (room = "large" OR children ≤ 15)`
`(children ≥ 10 AND children ≤ 30) AND (room = "small" OR children ≤ 15)`
`(children ≥ 10 AND children ≤ 30) AND (room = "large" OR children ≤ 15)`
explanation: The first part is a range check: 10 to 30 children. The second part applies the small room's limit: it is TRUE when the room is large, or when there are no more than 15 children. A valid booking must pass both parts, so they are joined with AND.
whyWrong: With OR, passing either part is enough, so 25 children in the small room are accepted, and so are 5.
`children ≥ 10 OR children ≤ 30` is TRUE for every number, so a booking for 40 children in the large room is accepted.
This applies the limit to the wrong room: 20 children are rejected in the large room but accepted in the small room.

stem: The online booking form at Tussock Lane Kitchen in Colac has two fields: the customer's name, which is required, and the number of guests, a whole number from 1 to 10. During alpha testing, the developer recorded the results shown. Which validation check do the results show is missing?
options: An existence check on the number of guests
A type check on the number of guests
An existence check on the customer's name
A range check on the number of guests
explanation: In test 2 the name is left blank, and the booking is saved instead of being rejected with a message. The form is missing an existence check on the name.
whyWrong: No test left the number of guests blank, so these results can't show whether that check is missing.
Test 3 shows "three" being rejected with the right message, so the type check is working.
Test 4 shows 12 being rejected with the right message, so a range check is present.

figures.title: Test table
rows: Guests must be a whole number
Guests must be a whole number

stem: Silvereye Singers, a community choir in Sale, takes concert bookings on paper forms, which a volunteer types into `bookings.csv`. Each line holds a name and a number of tickets. The booking program imports the file and applies three checks to each line: an existence check on the name, a type check that the number of tickets is a whole number, and a range check that it is from 1 to 10 inclusive. A line that fails any check is rejected and listed for the volunteer to correct. Which lines in the file shown are rejected?
options: Lines 2, 3 and 5
Lines 2, 3, 5 and 6
Lines 3, 5 and 6
Lines 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6
explanation: Line 2 has no name, so it fails the existence check. Lines 3 and 6 fail the type check, because `two` and 2.5 aren't whole numbers. Line 5 fails the range check, because 11 is above 10. Lines 1 and 4 hold the boundary values 1 and 10, which an inclusive range accepts.
whyWrong: Line 6 is also rejected: 2.5 isn't a whole number, so it fails the type check.
Line 2 is also rejected: it has no name, so it fails the existence check.
The range is inclusive, so 10 is accepted; line 4 passes every check.

stem: Which statement best describes alpha testing?
options: Testing by a selected group of real users in their own setting
Checking that data entered is reasonable before it is processed
Judging the finished solution against evaluation criteria after release
Testing by the developers before the solution is released to users
explanation: Alpha testing is done by the developers, or an in-house team, during development, to check that the solution works as designed before users see it.
whyWrong: This describes beta testing, which follows alpha testing.
This describes validation.
This describes evaluation, which takes place once the solution is in use.

stem: Kurrajong Kids Swim School in Horsham charges $18 per lesson, with 10% off the total when a family books 10 or more lessons. During alpha testing, the function shown is run with the test data in the test table. Which test's actual output will differ from its expected output?
options: Test 1
Test 2
Test 3
Test 4
explanation: Ten lessons should earn the discount, but line 3 tests `lessons > 10`, which is FALSE when `lessons` is 10. The function returns 180, not 162.00. The condition should be `lessons ≥ 10`.
whyWrong: 4 lessons get no discount, and the function correctly returns 4 × 18 = 72.
11 > 10 is TRUE, so the function correctly returns 198 × 0.9 = 178.20.
20 > 10 is TRUE, so the function correctly returns 360 × 0.9 = 324.

figures.code:
FUNCTION lessonCost(lessons)
    cost ← lessons * 18
    IF lessons > 10 THEN
        cost ← cost * 0.9
    ENDIF
    RETURN cost
ENDFUNCTION

stem: Hamid is alpha testing a program for Sunset Plains Grain in Ouyen that totals the tonnes delivered in 200 loads. The final total is wrong. He wants to see how the running total changes as each load is added, while the program runs to the end without stopping. Which technique suits best?
options: Setting a breakpoint on the line after the loop that totals the loads
Commenting out the loop so that only the first load's tonnes are totalled
Adding a debugging output statement inside the loop to show the total
Adding a range check that rejects any load outside the expected tonnes
explanation: A debugging output statement inside the loop shows the running total after every load without pausing the program, so Hamid can see where the total goes wrong.
whyWrong: A breakpoint pauses the program, and one after the loop shows only the final total, not each step.
Commenting out the loop removes the very processing he needs to watch.
A range check validates input; it doesn't show how the total changes.

stem: Wedgetail Archery Club in Seymour uses the function shown to find a competitor's highest score. Arrays are indexed from 0, and all scores are positive. Test 1, `highestScore([12, 18, 7, 15])`, returned 18, as expected. Which input for a second test would reveal the logic error in the function?
explanation: The loop on line 3 starts at 1, so `scores[0]` is never compared. With `[20, 18, 7, 15]` the function returns 18 instead of 20, which reveals the error. In the other inputs the highest score also appears after index 0, so the function still returns the right answer.
whyWrong: The highest score, 25, is at index 3, which the loop checks, so the function correctly returns 25.
The highest score, 14, is at index 2, which the loop checks, so the function correctly returns 14.
The same score appears at indexes 1 to 3, so the function still correctly returns 4.

figures.code:
FUNCTION highestScore(scores)
    highest ← 0
    FOR i ← 1 TO LENGTH(scores) - 1
        IF scores[i] > highest THEN
            highest ← scores[i]
        ENDIF
    ENDFOR
    RETURN highest
ENDFUNCTION

stem: Whipbird Hill Boarding Kennels in Benalla charges $25 a night for each dog, plus $10 a night for each dog that weighs over 30 kg. The function shown should work out one night's charge for a family's dogs from their weights in kilograms. Arrays are indexed from 0. During alpha testing, `nightlyCharge([12, 34, 8])` returns 95 instead of 85. Ash sets a breakpoint on line 6, which pauses the program each time line 6 is about to run. The table shows the values at each pause. What do the pauses show?
options: The loop makes one pass too many, so line 6 runs after the last dog
Line 6 runs for the 8 kg dog, so line 5 tests the wrong value
Line 4 adds the nightly rate twice for the dog that weighs 34 kg
Line 6 runs for every dog, so each dog is charged the extra $10
explanation: Line 6 should run only for a dog over 30 kg, but the second pause shows it about to run when `i` is 2, and `weights[2]` is 8. Line 5 compares the running total with 30 instead of the dog's weight, so once `total` passes 30, every later dog is charged the $10. Changing line 5 to `IF weights[i] > 30 THEN` makes the function return 85.
whyWrong: At the last pause `i` is 2, the last index of a three-element array, and the function returns without an error, so the loop runs the right number of times.
At the first pause `total` is 50, which is $25 for each of the first two dogs, so line 4 adds the rate once per dog.
The program pauses only twice, when `i` is 1 and 2; it doesn't pause for the 12 kg dog at index 0.

figures.code:
FUNCTION nightlyCharge(weights)
    total ← 0
    FOR i ← 0 TO LENGTH(weights) - 1
        total ← total + 25
        IF total > 30 THEN
            total ← total + 10
        ENDIF
    ENDFOR
    RETURN total
ENDFUNCTION

figures.title: Values at each pause on line 6

stem: The invoicing program at Nankeen Electrical in Traralgon has two modules written by different developers. `calculateFee` returns a job's fee in cents, for example 1250 for $12.50. `addGst` expects a fee in dollars and adds 10%. Each module passed every test in its own test table, but when the two modules were first run together, an invoice showed $1375.00 instead of $13.75. What does this show about alpha testing?
options: The test tables for both modules must have held incorrect expected outputs
Beta testing by real users should replace alpha testing for this program
Each module needed a range check on the fee it receives or returns
Modules must also be tested together, checking data passed between them
explanation: Each module worked correctly with its own test data. The error appears only when `calculateFee`'s output, in cents, is passed to `addGst`, which expects dollars: 1250 × 1.1 = 1375. Testing the modules together, and checking the values passed between them, finds this kind of error before users see it.
whyWrong: Each module does what its own design says, so its tests rightly passed; the fault lies in how the two modules fit together.
Beta testing follows alpha testing rather than replacing it, and users shouldn't be the first to find a calculation error.
1250 is a believable fee in dollars as well as in cents, so a range check wouldn't reliably catch the mismatch.

stem: Since a loyalty-points feature was added to the till program at Grey Fantail Café in Heathcote, the program crashes every time it prints a receipt. Kim comments out the single line that calls `addPoints(order)`, and receipts then print without a crash. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: The crash is caused by `addPoints` or by the data passed to it
The crash was a syntax error, which commenting out has corrected
The crash is in the receipt code, which runs differently without the line
The crash is a logic error, because the program ran before it stopped
explanation: Commenting out one line and seeing the crash stop narrows the search: the crash happens only when `addPoints` runs, so Kim should examine that function and the order data passed to it. She must restore the line once the error is fixed, or customers won't earn points.
whyWrong: Commenting out a line stops it running but doesn't correct anything, and the program runs normally until it prints a receipt, which points to a runtime error rather than a syntax error.
Receipts printed correctly before the feature was added and print again without the call, so the receipt code is unlikely to be the cause.
A logic error produces wrong output without stopping the program; a crash while the program runs is a runtime error.

stem: Which statement best describes beta testing?
options: Developers test each module with prepared test data during coding.
Intended users try a nearly complete solution in realistic conditions.
Users rate the solution against criteria after months of normal use.
Testers check that each value entered falls within an acceptable range.
explanation: Beta testing puts a nearly finished solution in the hands of people who match its intended users, in the conditions where it will be used, to find problems before release.
whyWrong: Developers testing modules with test data during coding is alpha testing.
Rating the solution against criteria after a period of use is evaluation, not testing.
Checking that values fall within an acceptable range describes a range check, a validation technique.

stem: Wemen Plains Grain Co-operative in the Mallee is having an app developed so that its 40 member farmers can book grain delivery times at the silo from their phones. Many members are older farmers with little experience of apps. Which group is most suitable for beta testing the app?
options: The four developers who wrote and debugged the app
The office staff who helped write the requirements
Eight member farmers with a range of ages and app experience
Twenty university students recruited through an advertisement
explanation: A beta test group should represent the people who will use the app. Member farmers of varying ages and experience will meet the same problems as the wider membership, including members who are unfamiliar with apps.
whyWrong: Developers already know how the app works, so they won't meet the problems farmers will. Testing by developers is alpha testing.
Office staff won't be booking deliveries, and they already know what the app is meant to do.
Students aren't the app's users and are likely to be more experienced with apps than many members.

stem: Soraya is preparing to beta test a booking app for Orchard Hill Physiotherapy in Ballarat. Which is the most appropriate scenario to give testers?
options: Book a 30-minute session with any physiotherapist next week.
Tap Book, choose Sam Lin, select 10:30, then tap Confirm.
Enter 32/13/2026 as the date to check that it is rejected.
Rate how satisfied you are with the app on a scale of 1 to 5.
explanation: A beta test scenario gives a realistic goal in the user's terms and leaves the tester to work out how to reach it. Observers can then see whether real users can complete the task unaided.
whyWrong: Listing each step tests whether the tester can follow instructions, not whether the interface is easy to use.
Entering an impossible date is a validation test with invalid data, which belongs in alpha testing.
A satisfaction rating is a survey question, not a task for the tester to carry out.

stem: During a beta test of a timesheet program for Coldwater Joinery in Wendouree, a tester can't work out how to submit a timesheet. The observing developer points to the Submit button so that the test can continue. What is the main problem with the developer's action?
options: The test becomes alpha testing because a developer took part in it.
The tester should have been given boundary test data to enter instead.
Observation should be replaced by a survey completed after the test.
The result no longer shows whether users can complete the task unaided.
explanation: Beta testing aims to find where real users struggle. Once the observer shows the tester the button, the scenario records a success that users working alone might not achieve, and the usability problem can be missed. The observer should record the difficulty without helping.
whyWrong: Observing a beta test doesn't turn it into alpha testing. The tester is still an intended user in realistic conditions.
Boundary test data checks how inputs are handled during alpha testing; it wouldn't show whether users can find features.
A survey would miss problems testers forget or don't report. Observation is the right technique if the observer doesn't help.

stem: Yambuk Cold Stores in Port Fairy is having a stock app developed for its warehouse staff, who will scan cartons with handheld scanners inside a freezer room while wearing thick gloves. Grace, the developer, plans to beta test the app with five warehouse staff on desktop computers in the office. Which change would most improve her beta test?
options: Have Grace's fellow developers carry out the scenarios instead of the warehouse staff
Give the warehouse staff a list of invalid inputs to type into each field of the app
Run the same scenarios on handheld scanners in the freezer room during a shift
Replace the scenarios with a survey that staff fill in after trying the app
explanation: Beta testing should happen in the conditions where the solution will really be used. On the scanners in the freezer room, with gloves on, testers will meet problems the office can't reveal, such as buttons too small to tap with a gloved finger.
whyWrong: Developers already know how the app works, and testing by developers is alpha testing.
Checking validation with prepared invalid data is the developers' job in alpha testing, and it would still happen in the office.
A survey loses the chance to observe real tasks, and the testing would still happen in the office.

stem: Talbot Ridge Dance School in Ballarat is having an app developed. Parents will use it to enrol their children in classes and pay fees, and the school's teachers will use it to mark attendance and message families. Which beta test plan is most suitable?
options: Some parents and some teachers, each given scenarios for their own role
Teachers only, because they understand how the school's classes are organised
Parents only, because parents will make up most of the app's users
Parents and teachers, all given the same scenarios so results can be compared
explanation: The app has two groups of users with different tasks. The beta test group should represent both, and each tester should carry out realistic scenarios for their own role, such as a parent enrolling a child in a Saturday class or a teacher marking the roll.
whyWrong: Teachers don't enrol children or pay fees, so problems parents meet would go unnoticed.
Leaving out teachers means real users never try the attendance and messaging features.
Parents don't mark attendance and teachers don't enrol children, so identical scenarios don't match what each group really does.

stem: Kororoit Creek Fitness in Melton beta tested its new class-booking app with eight members. The table shows the results. Which conclusion is best supported by the results?
options: The cancel function has a logic error, so it needs more alpha testing
Cancelling takes too long to process, so the app's response time must improve
Validation of card details failed, so it is the most urgent problem to fix
The Cancel option is hard to find, so its placement should be redesigned
explanation: Scenario 2 is the only one most testers couldn't finish without help, and the observer's note gives the reason: testers looked for Cancel under My account, but it is under Timetable. The long average time was spent searching, so the problem is where the option is placed, not how it works.
whyWrong: Nothing shows that cancelling gives a wrong result; most testers couldn't find the option.
The notes show the time was spent searching for the option, not waiting for the app.
The expired cards were rejected with a clear message, so the validation worked as intended.

figures.title: Beta test results (8 testers)
rows: 1. Book a spin class for next Tuesday
2. Cancel a class you have booked
Five testers opened My account looking for Cancel. It is under Timetable.
Two testers typed an expired card. The app rejected it with a clear message, and they corrected it.

stem: When should a new software solution normally be evaluated?
options: During coding, as each module is completed
Just before release, while beta testers use it
On the first day it is used by all its users
After it has been in normal use for some time
explanation: Evaluation judges how efficiently and effectively the solution performs in everyday use, so it waits until users are familiar with it and data about real use has built up.
whyWrong: Checking modules as they are completed is testing during development, not evaluation.
Users trying the solution before release is beta testing, which looks for problems to fix.
On the first day users are still learning, so the data would reflect the learning stage, not normal use.

stem: Harcourt Road Vets in Bendigo is planning how to evaluate its new online booking program. Which is the most suitable evaluation criterion?
options: At least 90% of online bookings are completed in under two minutes.
The program is written in an object-oriented programming language.
Clients will be surveyed six weeks after the program goes live.
The program must be fast and easy for clients to use at all times.
explanation: A good evaluation criterion is based on a requirement and is measurable. The program can log how long each online booking takes, so the percentage completed in under two minutes can be calculated and compared with the 90% target.
whyWrong: This describes how the program is built, not how well it performs for the clinic and its clients.
This is part of the timeline and data collection method, not a criterion to judge the program against.
'Fast and easy' has no measurable target, so the data can't show whether it has been met.

stem: What is the main purpose of an evaluation strategy?
options: To plan the tasks, durations and dependencies of the project
To plan which scenarios beta testers will complete before release
To plan how and when the solution will be judged against criteria
To plan the test data used to check the outputs of each module
explanation: An evaluation strategy plans the evaluation of the solution in use. It typically sets out the criteria, the data and how it is collected, the timing and who is responsible.
whyWrong: Tasks, durations and dependencies make up the project plan, such as a Gantt chart.
Scenarios for beta testers belong in a beta test plan, which is carried out before release.
Test data for checking module outputs belongs in a test table used during alpha testing.

stem: Mount Napier Office Supplies in Hamilton has written this evaluation strategy for its new online ordering program. What is the main weakness in the strategy?
options: Criterion 1 should be measured with a survey rather than system logs.
Criterion 2 relies on opinions instead of checking invoices for errors.
Criterion 3 should be measured by counting calculation errors instead.
Data for every criterion should be collected on the first day of use.
explanation: Whether invoices contain calculation errors is a matter of fact that can be checked by recalculating a sample of invoices. Staff opinions may be wrong or incomplete, so they don't give reliable evidence for criterion 2.
whyWrong: System logs give accurate times for every order; a survey would give only staff estimates.
Criterion 3 is about customers' views of ease of use, so a rating from customers suits it.
First-day data would reflect users learning the program, not its normal use.

figures.title: Evaluation strategy (extract)
rows: 1. Staff enter an order in under 3 minutes
Time from opening to saving each order
3. At least 80% of customers rate ordering 4 or 5 out of 5 for ease of use

stem: Tungamah Mower Repairs in Yarrawonga records warranty claims on paper forms and is replacing them with a claims program. One evaluation criterion is: 'The average time to process a warranty claim falls by at least 30%.' Which step must the evaluation strategy include so that this criterion can be applied?
options: Survey staff in the first week about how quickly the program processes claims
Time staff processing a sample of paper claims before the program starts
Ask staff after launch to estimate how long a paper claim used to take them
Beta test the program with the staff who process warranty claims each day
explanation: A fall of 30% can only be judged against a measured starting point. The paper process has to be timed before it is replaced, because once the program is in use the old times can no longer be measured.
whyWrong: First-week data reflects staff learning the program, and a survey gives opinions, not measured times.
Estimates made from memory are unreliable, so the comparison with the new times wouldn't be sound.
Beta testing finds problems before release; it doesn't measure how long the paper process took.

stem: Wonwondah Produce in Horsham has had a stock and dispatch app built by Farid, an external developer whose contract ends when the app is handed over in March. The table shows an extract from the evaluation strategy. What is the main weakness in the strategy?
options: Criterion 1's data should be collected from the day the app is handed over
Criterion 2 should compare the counts for every product, not a sample of 50
Criterion 3 should be measured with system logs instead of a questionnaire
Criterion 3 relies on someone who will no longer be working on the project
explanation: Farid's contract ends at the handover in March, but the questionnaire is due in June. Unless someone at Wonwondah Produce is made responsible for it, the drivers may never be surveyed and criterion 3 can't be applied. The other parts of the strategy are sound.
whyWrong: Data from the first weeks would reflect staff learning the app; May and June show normal use.
A random sample of 50 products is a practical way to estimate how accurate the stock levels are.
Ratings are the drivers' opinions, which system logs can't record, so a questionnaire suits criterion 3.

figures.title: Evaluation strategy (extract)
rows: 1. The average time to record a delivery is under 45 seconds
Time from first scan to saving each delivery
2. At least 95% of recorded stock levels match the shelves
Recorded and counted stock for 50 randomly chosen products
3. At least 80% of drivers rate the app 4 or 5 out of 5 for ease of use

stem: Which data collection technique is best suited to finding out why users dislike a new screen layout?
options: Analysing system logs of response times
Counting the errors in printed reports
Interviewing a small group of users
Timing how long each task takes users
explanation: Interviews let the evaluator ask follow-up questions and collect detailed qualitative data about users' reasons, which is what a 'why' question needs.
whyWrong: Response times show how fast the system is, not why users dislike the layout.
Counting report errors measures the accuracy of output, not users' views of a screen.
Timing tasks shows how long they take, but not the reasons behind users' opinions.

stem: Goulburn Plains Removals in Shepparton set this evaluation criterion for its new quoting program: 'The average time to create a quote is under 240 seconds.' The table shows the times the system log recorded for eight quotes. Which statement correctly applies the criterion to the data?
options: Met, because the average time is about 236 seconds
Not met, because the average time is about 249 seconds
Not met, because four quotes took 240 seconds or longer
Met, because the fastest quote took only 150 seconds
explanation: The eight times total 1890 seconds, and 1890 ÷ 8 = 236.25 seconds. The criterion sets a target for the average, and 236 seconds is under 240, so it is met.
whyWrong: About 249 seconds comes from leaving out the fastest quote. All eight recorded times count.
The criterion is about the average time, not about how many individual quotes were slow.
One fast quote says nothing about the average; the criterion needs all eight times.

figures.title: Quote times from the system log

stem: Norwood Street Library in Ballarat has a new catalogue and loans program. Which pairing of an evaluation criterion with a data collection technique is most appropriate?
options: Search results appear within 2 seconds: interview borrowers
Staff renew a loan in under 30 seconds: time each renewal
90% of borrowers rate the search as easy to use: system logs
No overdue notices are sent in error: survey borrowers' opinions
explanation: The criterion sets a time target, so timing staff as they renew loans measures exactly what the criterion states.
whyWrong: Borrowers can't accurately report a response time of 2 seconds; it needs timing or system logs.
Ratings are opinions, which system logs can't record; a survey is needed.
Whether notices were sent in error is checked by comparing notices with loan records, not by opinion.

stem: Tarrawingee Cycles in Wangaratta set this criterion for its new service-booking app: 'At least 85% of survey respondents rate the app 4 or 5 out of 5.' The table shows the survey results. Which statement correctly applies the criterion to the data?
options: Met, because the average rating is above 4 out of 5
Met, because 92.5% of respondents gave a rating of 3 or more
Not met, because only 35% of respondents gave the top rating of 5
Not met, because 82.5% of respondents gave a rating of 4 or 5
explanation: 33 of the 40 respondents (14 + 19) rated the app 4 or 5, which is 82.5%. The target is at least 85%, so the criterion is not met.
whyWrong: The average is about 4.1, but the criterion sets a target for the percentage rating 4 or 5, not for the average.
Ratings of 3 don't count; the criterion specifies ratings of 4 or 5.
Ratings of 4 also count towards the target, so 35% is the wrong figure to apply.

stem: Wychitella Freight in Bendigo set this criterion for its new dispatch program: 'No more than 2% of printed labels have an incorrect address.' In weeks 5 to 8 after launch, the program printed 1 200 labels. Staff checked a random sample of 250 of them against the customers' orders and found 6 with an incorrect address. Which statement correctly applies the criterion to the data?
options: Met, because 6 errors are only 0.5% of the 1 200 labels printed
Not met, because 2.4% of the sampled labels had a wrong address
Met, because an error rate of 2.4% rounds down to the 2% target
Met, because 244 correct labels are more than 98% of the sample
explanation: 6 ÷ 250 = 0.024, so 2.4% of the sampled labels were wrong. A random sample stands for all the labels printed, so the best estimate of the error rate is 2.4%, which is more than the 2% allowed. The criterion is not met.
whyWrong: Only 250 labels were checked, so the other 950 may hold errors too; the rate must come from the sample.
'No more than 2%' is a limit, and 2.4% is above it. Rounding doesn't change that.
98% of 250 is 245, so 244 correct labels (97.6%) falls just short of 98%.

stem: Before launching a returns program, Toolamba Outdoor Gear in Shepparton timed staff processing returns by hand, and the average was 8.0 minutes. In weeks 5 to 8 after launch, the program's log gave an average of 6.2 minutes. The criterion is: 'The average time to process a return falls by at least 25%.' Which statement correctly applies the criterion?
options: Met, because the average time fell by about 29%
Met, because the new average is lower than the old one
Met, because 6.2 minutes is within 25% of 8.0 minutes
Not met, because the average time fell by 22.5%
explanation: The average fell by 8.0 − 6.2 = 1.8 minutes. As a percentage of the original time, 1.8 ÷ 8.0 = 22.5%, which is less than the 25% required, so the criterion is not met. A 25% fall would have needed an average of 6.0 minutes or less.
whyWrong: 29% divides the fall by the new time (1.8 ÷ 6.2); a fall is measured against the original 8.0 minutes.
Any fall at all makes the new average lower; the criterion needs a fall of at least 25%.
Being within 25% of the old time isn't the same as falling by at least 25%, which needs 6.0 minutes or less.

stem: Rokewood Community Car Share has 300 members, who book its cars through a new app. To apply the criterion 'At least 80% of members find the app easy to use', the coordinator surveyed the 25 members who had phoned the help line about the app. Which change would make the evaluation data most reliable?
options: Survey a random sample of all members who have booked with the app
Survey the volunteers who answer the help line about the calls they took
Ask the same 25 members to fill in the survey again a month later
Count how many calls the help line receives about the app each week
explanation: Members who phoned the help line are the ones who had trouble, so they don't represent the membership. A random sample of members who have used the app gives results that stand for all of them, so the percentage can fairly be compared with 80%.
whyWrong: Volunteers can only pass on what callers told them, not whether members in general find the app easy.
Surveying the same 25 again still leaves out every member who never needed help.
A count of calls doesn't show what percentage of members find the app easy to use.

stem: Saltbush Solar in Mildura is having an invoicing program developed. The Gantt chart shows the plan, in days. The lead developer falls ill, and Code interface takes 3 days longer than planned. To recover time, the project manager adds a second tester so that Integrate and test takes 2 days instead of 4. Compared with the original plan, when is the handover?
options: On time
1 day late
3 days late
5 days late
explanation: The critical path is Analyse requirements → Design interface → Code interface → Integrate and test → Beta test, giving a handover on day 24. The 3-day delay means Code interface finishes on day 20 instead of day 17, so Integrate and test starts on day 21 instead of day 18. Shortening it by 2 days recovers 2 of those days, so the handover is on day 25, 1 day late.
whyWrong: The 2 days saved in testing don't fully cover the 3-day delay to a critical task.
3 days late ignores the 2 days recovered by shortening Integrate and test.
5 days late adds the 2 days to the delay instead of subtracting them.

stem: Halfway through the development of a rostering program for Silverleaf Aged Care in Warragul, the only developer who has worked on the payroll module leaves the team. Which practice, if followed from the start of the project, would most reduce the resulting delay?
options: Adding validation checks to every input in the payroll module
Beta testing the payroll module with a group of care staff
Setting measurable evaluation criteria for the payroll module
Documenting the payroll module's code and progress throughout
explanation: When the only person who knows a module leaves, a replacement must learn it before work can continue. Internal documentation and up-to-date progress records let them understand the code and pick up where it was left, so less time is lost.
whyWrong: Validation improves the quality of input data but doesn't help a new developer understand the module.
Beta testing finds problems users meet; it doesn't pass on the departing developer's knowledge.
Evaluation criteria are used to judge the finished solution, not to continue its development.

stem: Murray Bend Pharmacy in Echuca is having a stock program developed. The Gantt chart shows the plan, in days. Which event, on its own, would delay the handover?
options: Design stock screens takes 1 more day than planned
Code report module takes 3 more days than planned
Design reports takes 2 more days than planned
The two report tasks take 3 more days between them
explanation: The critical path is Gather requirements → Design stock screens → Code stock module → Alpha testing → Beta testing, taking 18 days, so any delay to a task on it delays the handover. The report tasks are due to finish on day 10, but Alpha testing can't start until Code stock module finishes on day 13, so up to 3 extra days on the report path don't move the handover.
whyWrong: Code report module would finish on day 13, the same day as Code stock module, so Alpha testing still starts on time.
Design reports would finish on day 7 and Code report module on day 12, before Alpha testing is due to start.
Between them these add 3 days, so the report path finishes on day 13, the same day as Code stock module, and Alpha testing still starts on day 14.

stem: Joel Joel Equine Clinic near Stawell is having a booking app developed. The Gantt chart shows the plan, in days. Mateo, who will code the database, is to be moved to another project for a few days partway through that task, so Code database (E) will finish late. What is the longest Code database can be delayed without delaying go-live?
options: 0 days
1 day
3 days
7 days
explanation: The critical path is A, B, D, G and H, with go-live at the end of day 23. Code database is due to finish at the end of day 13, but Integrate and alpha test (G) can't start until Code booking screens (D) finishes at the end of day 16. Code database can finish up to 3 days later, at the end of day 16, without holding up G, so go-live stays at day 23.
whyWrong: Code database isn't on the critical path, so a short delay to it doesn't move go-live.
1 day compares only the two coding tasks (7 − 6) and ignores that Design database finishes 2 days before Design booking screens.
7 days measures up to the start of Beta test, but G can't start until Code database has finished.

stem: Halfway through the coding of a delivery app for Gypsum Creek Couriers in Mildura, the publisher of the mapping library the app uses withdraws it. The developers must switch to another library and rewrite the map screens. The client's requirements haven't changed. Which statement best describes the effect on the project plan?
options: Scope creep has occurred, so the agreed scope must be rewritten first
A technical issue has added unplanned work, so later tasks may slip
The plan is unaffected, because the app's requirements haven't changed
Only the testing tasks are affected, as the new library must be tested
explanation: Losing a library the app depends on is a technical issue. Choosing a replacement, rewriting the map screens and retesting them are work the plan didn't allow for, so coding takes longer, and if coding is on the critical path, later tasks and the handover slip.
whyWrong: Scope creep is growth in what the solution must do. The requirements are unchanged; only the way of meeting them has changed.
The requirements are the same, but the work needed to meet them has grown, and the plan has no time for it.
Rewriting the map screens is coding work, so coding takes longer before testing even starts.

stem: Moonambel Music School near Avoca needs its new lesson-booking program, used by families and teachers, running by the first day of Term 1, a date that can't move. Scope creep during coding has used up 6 days, so the project manager plans to hold the date by cutting beta testing from 6 days to none. What is the most likely consequence?
options: The critical path becomes longer, so the program misses Term 1 anyway
The added features are dropped, which reverses the effect of the scope creep
Nothing is lost, because alpha testing has already checked every module
Problems that families and teachers would have found appear after launch
explanation: Cutting beta testing keeps the date, but the time lost to scope creep is taken from quality. Problems that only real users in real conditions would reveal are found after launch, when families and teachers already depend on the program.
whyWrong: Cutting a task shortens the path it is on; it can't make the critical path longer.
Cutting a test doesn't remove the features that were added; that work has already been done.
Alpha testing checks modules against test data; it can't show how real users manage with the program.

stem: Which record would most help a developer explain, at the end of a project, why coding took longer than planned?
options: The software requirements specification
The evaluation criteria for the solution
A test table of the expected and actual outputs
A dated development journal kept during coding
explanation: A journal kept during coding records problems, decisions and changes as they happened, so it shows the causes of the delay.
whyWrong: The SRS states what the solution must do; it doesn't record what happened during coding.
Evaluation criteria are for judging the finished solution, not for recording progress.
A test table records test results, not why coding tasks took longer than planned.

stem: Ashleigh manages the development of a stock program for Tidewater Seafoods in Portland. Coding has finished 3 days late because the client's price data arrived late. How should she record this on the project's Gantt chart?
options: Replace the planned dates with the actual dates so the chart stays current
Annotate the actual finish date and the cause, keeping the planned dates visible
Leave the chart unchanged, because it shows the plan the client agreed to
Delete the coding task and add a new task with its actual duration instead
explanation: An annotation records what actually happened and why, while keeping the original plan visible. Planned and actual dates can then be compared when the project plan is assessed.
whyWrong: Overwriting the planned dates loses the original plan, so planned and actual can't be compared later.
An unchanged chart doesn't record progress, and the tasks that depend on coding won't be rescheduled.
Deleting the task loses the planned duration and gives no reason for the delay.

stem: Which feature of project management software is most useful when a task runs late?
options: Moving dependent tasks and recalculating the critical path automatically
Checking that each date entered is in the correct format before saving
Storing each version of the source code in a shared online repository
Surveying users about the solution once it has been released for use
explanation: When a task runs late, every task that depends on it may need to move. The software reschedules them and shows whether the critical path, and so the finish date, has changed.
whyWrong: Checking the format of dates is validation; it doesn't show the effect of a delay on the plan.
Storing versions of code is version control, which doesn't reschedule tasks.
Surveying users after release is part of evaluating the solution, not tracking the project.

stem: Little Wrens Childcare in Frankston is having an enrolment program developed. The Gantt chart shows the plan, in days. Code forms finishes 2 days later than planned. Which adjustment, on its own, would still let the program go live on the planned day?
options: Add a developer so Code reports takes 2 days instead of 4
Add a tester so Beta test takes 2 days instead of 3
Add two testers so Alpha test takes 1 day instead of 3
Use a template so Design reports takes 1 day instead of 2
explanation: Code forms is on the critical path (Collect requirements → Design forms → Code forms → Alpha test → Beta test), so the 2-day delay moves go-live from day 19 to day 21. Only a saving of at least 2 days on a later critical task recovers it: cutting Alpha test from 3 days to 1 brings go-live back to day 19.
whyWrong: Code reports isn't on the critical path, so finishing it sooner doesn't bring Alpha test forward.
Saving 1 day on Beta test recovers only half of the delay, so go-live would be on day 20.
Design reports isn't on the critical path, so shortening it has no effect on go-live.

stem: Four developers building a quoting program for Eurack Solar in Geelong keep journals. The table shows one entry from each. Which entry would be most useful when the project plan is assessed at the end of the project?
options: Priya's entry
Tom's entry
Anh's entry
Kai's entry
explanation: Anh's entry records the date, the time spent, the task, a problem and its cause (a rule missing from the SRS), the decision taken and why, and the next step. If the quote screen later runs late, this entry explains why.
whyWrong: It has no date or time spent, and 'some problems' doesn't say what went wrong or why.
It records the task and time spent but no problems, decisions or next steps.
It gives no time spent, and a feeling about progress isn't evidence of what happened.

stem: Moliagul Bike Hire in Maldon is having a booking system developed. At the end of day 12, the project manager annotated the plan with each task's progress, as shown in the table. If each task continues at its planned rate from now on, which task's progress will delay go-live?
options: Code bookings
Code staff reports
Load test data
Write user guide
explanation: Turn each gap into days. Code bookings is 20% of 10 days = 2 days behind, Code staff reports is 60% of 5 = 3 days, Load test data is 25% of 4 = 1 day, and Write user guide is 50% of 8 = 4 days. Only Code bookings is further behind than it can afford, because it can't finish late at all, so go-live moves 2 days later. The other tasks will finish late, but within the time they have to spare.
whyWrong: It is the furthest behind in percentage terms (60%, or 3 days of work), but it can finish up to 4 days late without delaying go-live.
It should already have finished, but it is only 1 day behind and can finish up to 5 days late.
It hasn't started and is 4 days behind, but it can finish up to 5 days late.
